summary:
Visitors in Normandie stand under France's national framework: the rules on identity documents, anti-discrimination, criminal law and marriage apply uniformly across all regions and divisions, and the sources reviewed contain no division-specific transgender findings for this region. The national mechanisms they document operate here unchanged.

Prison placement follows no dedicated statute. Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code requires men and women to be held in separate establishments, so trans women whose identity documents record a male sex, the majority of those held, are placed in men's facilities. BuzzFeed News reported on 12 January 2018 that one detainee recalled other inmates shouting that they did not want women on the wing, alongside threats of violence. Adeline Hazan, controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty, states that transgender detainees, overwhelmingly women, are the group that suffers the most in prison; the same feature describes the 'worrying' conditions of an American trans woman, Kara B., held in custody.

The CGLPL, France's national preventive mechanism, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, following its opinion of 30 June 2010. It records serious violations of trans detainees' fundamental rights persisting in adult prisons. The review covered some forty transgender detainees, with interviews including eight trans women and one trans man, and inspection visits at the Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station; Caen falls within this region, while the remaining establishments do not. No comparable violations were noted in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres.

The 2021 opinion records placement by birth sex, isolation and exposure during strip searches as persistent violations, and found no marked improvement since 2010 despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform. The CGLPL issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty and identified structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention, resting on a decade of letters from detained trans people. Coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October; her incarceration was raised before the French National Assembly in oral question no. 219 to the Keeper of the Seals, arguing that the prison system cannot guarantee conditions for trans detainees.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of questioning by French border police at an airport, carried out in front of other travellers and documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The Défenseur des droits issued a framework decision on trans rights confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the baseline is the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.
tangentialFactors:
The documented risk concentrates in two settings, detention and the border, rather than in everyday movement, accommodation or services, where France's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition. A trans visitor who is not entering or leaving the country and is not detained therefore faces a materially different exposure profile from a trans resident who is.

Age and institutional setting shape the findings. The CGLPL recorded no comparable violations in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres during the same review, which isolates the adult prison system as the site of the persistent failures.

The two recent opinions frame the persistence question differently. The 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, which the CGLPL gave as its reason for returning to the subject in 2021 alongside the changes brought by the 2016 gender-recognition law and its terminology, and the extension of coverage to intersex and non-binary detainees.

Border practice in France has a documented first-person precedent dating to 2017, whereas the deployment of identity-document checks against trans travellers has not been separately quantified in the sources reviewed.

outOfScopeNotes:
No division-specific enforcement data for Normandie is available in the sources reviewed: there is no record of how many trans detainees have been held in the region's establishments, how placement decisions were made locally, or whether any complaint has been lodged there. The Caen inspection visit is the only establishment from the CGLPL's 2021 review located in this region, and the outcome of that individual visit is not broken out.

The date of the Défenseur des droits' framework decision on trans rights is not stated in the inventory and remains unresolved; only its content, its use of the 2023 EU Fundamental Rights Agency survey, and its guidance to service providers are sourced.

Whether the binding guidance issued by the CGLPL on 25 May 2021 has changed placement practice after 2025 is not established here. The Louna case shows the practice continuing through 2025, but no post-2025 compliance reporting appears in the sources.

The claim that the vast majority of trans women detainees lack sex-reassignment surgery, and therefore hold male-marked documents, derives from the BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 and has not been re-verified against more recent ministry data.

Border-document checks against trans travellers rest on a single first-person account of 7 March 2017; no statistics on the frequency of such checks at French entry points are sourced.
